Field observations of the Woodlark (Lullula arborea) provide detailed insights into the early developmental stages of this species. When eggs are incubated at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the age at hatching is approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a period that aligns closely with the incubation durations reported for other Alaudidae of comparable egg size. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet body mass of just 2.79 grams [Ww0 = 2.79 grams], a value that reflects the considerable energetic demands of the subsequent nestling phase. This initial mass, typical of altricial young, is followed by a rapid growth trajectory fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. The nestling period concludes with fledging, which, under the thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that characterize the active metabolic phase for adults, occurs at 18.5 days after hatching [tx = 18.5 days after hatching]. This relatively short time to flight attainment is a critical life-history transition for the altricial nestling, marking the end of its complete dependence on the nest structure.

Sexual maturation in the Woodlark occurs several weeks after the fledgling achieves independent flight. Under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], puberty is attained at 55.5 days after hatching [tp = 55.5 days after hatching]. The maximum lifespan recorded for the Woodlark in the wild stands at approximately 8.2 years [am = approximately 8.2 years], a longevity that is relatively high for a bird of this size and which was documented under the typical thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Over the course of this extended life, females exhibit a consistent reproductive output. Investigations into the species' breeding ecology reveal that a female typically produces one to two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to two eggs per clutch] and that she may successfully raise up to two clutches per year [F_R_i = up to two clutches per year] under favorable seasonal conditions. This moderate reproductive rate is characteristic of a life-history strategy that balances annual fecundity against adult survival, enabling populations to persist even when fledging success varies considerably across years.

Adult body mass in the Woodlark shows a modest degree of sexual dimorphism. The ultimate wet weight attained by breeding females averages 26.3 grams [Wwi = 26.3 grams], while males, which are typically slightly heavier in this species, reach an average of 27.4 grams [Wwi = 27.4 grams]. This difference in mass is likely related to the energetic demands of egg production in females and the competitive pressures of territory defense and song posturing in males. The basal metabolic rate of the Woodlark, measured under post-absorptive, resting conditions at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 103 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 103 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This level of metabolic intensity is consistent with the allometric predictions for a passerine of this adult mass and reflects the high daily energetic costs of sustaining the species' active, ground-foraging lifestyle.

Comparative analyses across the Alaudidae family highlight the Woodlark's intermediate position regarding several life-history traits. For this species, incubation at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] results in hatching after exactly 14 days [ab = 14 days], a duration that is marginally longer than that observed in several smaller-bodied alaudids which may hatch in as few as 11 days. The 18.5-day fledging period (18.5 days after hatching) [tx = 18.5 days after hatching] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] is similarly on the longer end of the range for the family, possibly reflecting a strategy of producing slightly more developed young at nest departure. The body mass at hatching of 2.79 grams [Ww0 = 2.79 grams] represents a small proportion of the adult female mass of 26.3 grams [Wwi = 26.3 grams], a ratio typical of altricial species that exhibit a high degree of parental care. Males, in contrast, achieve a stable body mass of 27.4 grams [Wwi = 27.4 grams], a difference attributed to the demands of territory defense and song display. The documented maximum lifespan of 8.2 years [am = 8.2 years] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] places the Woodlark among the longer-lived members of its genus, a trait that likely buffers populations against occasional years of poor reproductive success.
